paras: The threatened lynching of J. A. Gafford was a threat by residents of Coal Hill, Arkansas, in March 1888 to hang the warden of the town's convict mining camp after an inquest blamed him for the deaths of convicts. No attempt on him was reported; he fled, was captured in November and was convicted of second-degree murder at Clarksville in December. The threat reached the national press as the closing line of wire stories about convict abuse, and a later dispatch forecast a "double lynching" that did not take place.

Coal Hill was a mining town where the mines were worked by convict labor, and Gafford had been warden of the camp for about three months. According to an Arkansas Gazette account, he had a convict named Charles Williams chained to a whipping post on February 22 and given 400 lashes, and Williams died the next day. Guards testified that Gafford made convicts fight, and one of them, Mose Harvey, died a week after being kicked by another convict, Mat Bailey.
Coroner Blythe's jury found that Williams "came to his death from cruel treatment inflicted by J. A. Gafford." Blythe swore out a warrant, but Gafford had left for Little Rock and then Memphis.

A St. Louis dispatch dated March 12 said that as the investigation went on, "the citizens of Coal Hill are much excited and threaten to hang Grafford and tear down the prison barracks." A Little Rock dispatch of March 13 said the people "threaten to lynch Grafford," and a Missouri paper said they "wanted to lynch" the warden. The fuller accounts of the inquest do not mention a threat, and none of the reports describes a crowd gathering.

On March 21 a St. Louis Post-Dispatch special said the people of Coal Hill were "worked up to a furore" and that there was "promise of a double lynching very soon." It said the warden, named as "Clifford," was in the sheriff's hands and would be brought to the Coal Hill jail, where the people were also demanding George Crisp, a man held at Ozark on a charge of assaulting an eight-year-old girl. A Little Rock brief likewise placed both men in jail at Coal Hill "in danger of being lynched."

Governor Hughes offered a $200 reward for Gafford's delivery to the sheriff of Johnson county and visited the camp with the Penitentiary Board, which found that an earlier warden, Scott, had been even more cruel. A Coal Hill dispatch of March 22 still called Gafford "the fugitive."

In November he was captured at Cumberland Gap, Tennessee, under indictment for the deaths of three convicts. An Arkansas news column reported "a strong feeling against him at Coal Hill," but said he was believed safe from lynch law in the Clarksville jail. On December 8 he was convicted of second-degree murder on one count and sentenced to five years in the penitentiary.

The first St. Louis wire ran on March 13 in papers from Wheeling to Salt Lake City and Savannah under headlines such as "INHUMAN TREATMENT" and "Horrible, if True." These stories centered on the beatings, and the lynching threat appeared only in their last sentence. The Nevada County Picayune reprinted the Gazette account under "PRISON REFORM NEEDED," calling Gafford "the wretch" and making no mention of the threat.

The March 21 special was framed around a coming lynching, under headlines including "HANGING BEE PROBABLE," "Prospects of a Lynching" and, in the Wichita Eagle, "JUST INDIGNATION." The Wheeling Register headed it "Expected When Two Brutal Murderers Reach Coal Hill," grouping the warden with the accused assailant. No Black-press coverage survives from 1888, and the white papers did not report what became of the forecast.
The trial result ran in December as one-line briefs, which variously named the warden "J. A. Gifford," "John A. Gifford" and "J. F. Gifford."

The March 21 report that the warden was in the sheriff's custody conflicts with the Coal Hill dispatch of the next day and with November reports calling him a fugitive since March. The camp's county is given as Johnson in the reward notice and the Arkansas news column, but as Jefferson in one November dispatch.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of J. A. Gafford
bases: Wire reports said Coal Hill citizens threatened to hang or lynch the convict-camp warden after convicts died under his charge (A1, A18, A22); no attack on him is reported, so this is a threatened lynching only.

Nobody was killed: the warden fled, was captured in November and was tried and sentenced at Clarksville (A33, A34, A35). The townspeople's threat to hang him was a threat of extralegal punishment for the convict deaths (A1, A18), but no crowd is reported to have gathered or acted.

Two separate dispatches (St. Louis and Little Rock, Mar 12-13) report the threat (A1, A18), and a separate Post-Dispatch special of Mar 21 repeats it (A22, A23). The fuller coroner's-jury and Arkansas Gazette accounts do not mention a lynching threat (A8, A21).

accounts.label: Coroner's jury / Arkansas Gazette
accounts.gist: The jury found Williams died from Gafford's cruelty; Gafford had already left for Little Rock and Memphis; no lynching threat is mentioned.

accounts.label: Post-Dispatch special (Mar 21)
accounts.gist: Clifford was said to be in the sheriff's hands and headed for Coal Hill jail, where a 'double lynching' with George Crisp was forecast.

accounts.label: Arkansas state news (Nov)
accounts.gist: Gafford was captured in Kentucky/Tennessee and returned; feeling ran strong at Coal Hill, but he was thought safe in the Clarksville jail.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the St. Louis wire as a convict-abuse story under headlines such as 'INHUMAN TREATMENT', 'Horrible, if True' and 'HORRORS OF THE MINES', with the lynching threat as its closing line.
The Nevada County Picayune reprinted the Gazette account to argue 'Arkansas needs prison reform', calling Gafford 'the wretch'; it condemned the warden, not the threatened mob.
The Mar 21 special treated a lynching as expected, under headlines 'HANGING BEE PROBABLE', 'Prospects of a Lynching' and, in the Wichita Eagle, 'JUST INDIGNATION'.
